metadata.name: crontab
metadata.description: Schedule commands to run periodically at fixed times, dates, or intervals

installation.note: crontab is part of cron package, typically pre-installed on Ubuntu systems

overview.summary: crontab manages cron jobs - scheduled tasks that run automatically at specified times. It allows you to edit, list, and remove scheduled jobs. Cron jobs are essential for automation, backups, maintenance tasks, and periodic system operations.
when_to_use: Run reports or data processing jobs

syntax.description: Manage cron jobs. Without options, opens editor to edit current user's crontab. Use -l to list, -r to remove, -e to edit.

options.use_case: Add, modify, or remove scheduled jobs

options.description: Remove the current user's crontab (deletes all jobs)
options.use_case: Delete all scheduled jobs (use with caution)

examples.title: List current cron jobs
examples.description: Display all scheduled cron jobs for the current user
examples.output:
# Edit this file to introduce tasks to be run by cron.
# Each task to run has to be defined through a single line
# indicating with different fields when the task will be run
# and what command to run for the task
#
# m h  dom mon dow   command
0 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
*/15 * * * * /usr/bin/check_disk.sh
0 0 1 * * /usr/bin/monthly_report.sh

elements.meaning: Minute (0-59), Hour (0-23), Day of month (1-31), Month (1-12), Day of week (0-7, where 0 and 7 = Sunday)
Wildcard meaning 'every' (every minute, every hour, etc.)
The command or script to execute

output_explanation.notes: Each line represents one scheduled job. Empty lines and comments are allowed.

examples.use_case: Review what jobs are currently scheduled

examples.title: Edit crontab
examples.description: Open crontab in default editor to add or modify jobs

elements.meaning: Opens in your default editor (usually nano, vim, or vi)
Save changes and exit editor to apply new schedule

output_explanation.notes: After saving, cron automatically reloads the crontab. No restart needed.

examples.use_case: Add new scheduled jobs or modify existing ones

examples.title: Common cron schedule examples
examples.description: Examples of common cron schedule patterns
examples.output:
# Run every minute
* * * * * /path/to/command

# Run every hour at minute 0
0 * * * * /path/to/command

# Run daily at 2:30 AM
30 2 * * * /path/to/command

# Run every Monday at 9:00 AM
0 9 * * 1 /path/to/command

# Run on the 1st of every month at midnight
0 0 1 * * /path/to/command

# Run every 15 minutes
*/15 * * * * /path/to/command

# Run every weekday (Monday-Friday) at 5:00 PM
0 17 * * 1-5 /path/to/command

elements.meaning: Every minute of every hour of every day
At minute 0 of every hour (top of each hour)

output_explanation.notes: Always use absolute paths for commands and scripts in crontab. Environment variables may differ.

common_misconceptions.title: Cron runs in user's environment
common_misconceptions.misconception: Cron jobs run with the same environment as your interactive shell
common_misconceptions.reality: Cron runs with a minimal environment. PATH may be limited, and shell variables may not be set. Always use absolute paths.
common_misconceptions.tip: Use absolute paths for all commands and scripts. Set PATH and other variables in the crontab if needed.

common_misconceptions.title: Cron needs to be restarted
common_misconceptions.misconception: You need to restart cron service after editing crontab
common_misconceptions.reality: Cron automatically reloads crontabs when they're saved. No restart needed.
common_misconceptions.tip: Just save your crontab - changes take effect immediately

common_pitfalls.description: Using relative paths for commands or scripts fails because cron's working directory is different
common_pitfalls.solution: Always use absolute paths: /usr/local/bin/script.sh instead of ./script.sh

common_pitfalls.description: Cron job output goes to email or is discarded if email isn't configured
Cron doesn't have your shell's environment variables
common_pitfalls.solution: Set variables in crontab: PATH=/usr/bin:/usr/local/bin or source profile: * * * * * source ~/.bashrc && command

best_practices: Always use absolute paths for commands and scripts
Redirect output to log files for debugging: >> /var/log/job.log 2>&1
Test commands manually before adding to crontab
Use descriptive comments in crontab to document what each job does
Set PATH and other needed environment variables at the top of crontab
Use systemd timers for more complex scheduling needs (modern alternative)
performance_tips: Avoid scheduling too many jobs at the same time to prevent system load
Use */N syntax carefully - */1 runs every minute, which may be too frequent
Consider using systemd timers for jobs that need more control or dependencies
Monitor cron job execution in /var/log/syslog or with journalctl -u cron

related_commands.description: at schedules commands to run once at a specific time, while crontab is for recurring jobs
systemd timers are a modern alternative to cron with more features (dependencies, better logging)
watch runs commands repeatedly in the foreground, while cron runs in background at scheduled times

additional_notes.note1: Cron jobs run with minimal environment. Set PATH, HOME, and other variables in crontab if needed
additional_notes.note2: Cron logs are typically in /var/log/syslog. Check with: grep CRON /var/log/syslog
additional_notes.note3: For system-wide cron jobs, use /etc/crontab or files in /etc/cron.d/ (requires root)
additional_notes.note4: Day of week: 0 and 7 = Sunday, 1 = Monday, 2 = Tuesday, etc.
